idiom_name: memo table keyed by (rule, position) + one lookup/store wrapper per rule
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep the grammar as mutually recursive functions of the input position and wrap every one of them in the same prologue/epilogue - look up (rule, position) in a per-parse table, and on a miss evaluate the rule body and store the result, success or failure, under that key. Positions are bounded by the input length, so the table can be dense (one row per rule, n+1 columns) or hashed on a packed integer key, and the entry must distinguish 'not yet computed' from 'computed and failed', because the recorded failures are what remove the repeated-failing-alternative blow-up. Size the table from the input, own it per parse and drop it with the input. Keep the memoized rules pure: any rule that reads parser state (indentation, type-name or symbol tables, semantic predicates) must leave the memoized set or have that state folded into the key, and left recursion must be rewritten into a right-recursive form or handled by a seed-growing algorithm. The classic structure - a memo-table object with explicit rule/position keys, a rule registry and its own lifecycle - is still justified when several entry points or tools share one grammar, when the table itself is a product (diagnostics, incremental reuse), or when the language gives no cheap way to attach the cache to the rules.
code_sketch:
memo = table[rule][position]                 # one row per rule, n+1 columns

function rule(id, pos):
    entry = memo.lookup(id, pos)
    if entry.is_computed: return entry.result  # success OR recorded failure
    value = rule_body(id, pos)                 # ordinary backtracking descent
    memo.store(id, pos, value)                 # failures cached as failures
    return value

parse(input):
    memo = new table(rules, len(input) + 1)
    return rule(start, 0)
pitfalls: Folding nothing but the position into the memo key although the rule reads parser state, so every state change is answered from a stale entry.
Caching only successes, which leaves the repeated failing alternatives - the actual source of the exponential blow-up - uncached.
Keeping the table alive after the parse or sharing it between parses, turning a per-parse cache into an unbounded, cross-input-contaminated store.

Wrong move: enable packrat caching on a predictive or low-backtracking grammar -> memo-table lookups and O(n) storage can outweigh avoided work -> instead benchmark plain recursive descent and memoize only where repeated backtracking dominates.
